stem:
A 32-year-old at 30 weeks gestation has painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound suggests placenta previa.

Which action should be avoided?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Frequent observations are essential to detect haemodynamic deterioration in antepartum haemorrhage and pose no risk to the placenta.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Inserting a finger through the os into a praevia can precipitate massive haemorrhage, which is why placental localisation precedes any digital exam.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Continuous CTG is essential to assess fetal wellbeing in antepartum haemorrhage and does not contact the placenta.

options.label: D
options.explanation: A careful speculum exam visualises the cervix and excludes local causes without disturbing the placenta.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice — it confirms praevia and guides management without mechanical risk.

context:
When the placenta covers or sits very close to the internal cervical os, the lower segment is highly vascular and easily disturbed.

Any woman with antepartum bleeding should have a transabdominal/transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta before any digital vaginal examination is considered.
